01

Lagrange Multipliers

Lesson 17 · §15.8
Don't know this yet? §s158 in the full guide →
From the official study guide

Method of Lagrange Multipliers

To find the extreme values of f(x,y)f(x,y)f(x,y) subject to a constraint g(x,y)=kg(x,y) = kg(x,y)=k, solve the system:

∇f=λ ∇gandg(x,y)=k\nabla f = \lambda\,\nabla g \qquad \text{and} \qquad g(x,y) = k∇f=λ∇gandg(x,y)=k

That is:

  • fx=λ gxf_x = \lambda\, g_xfx​=λgx​
  • fy=λ gyf_y = \lambda\, g_yfy​=λgy​
  • g(x,y)=kg(x,y) = kg(x,y)=k

Three Variables

To optimize f(x,y,z)f(x,y,z)f(x,y,z) subject to g(x,y,z)=kg(x,y,z) = kg(x,y,z)=k:

∇f=λ ∇gandg(x,y,z)=k\nabla f = \lambda\,\nabla g \qquad \text{and} \qquad g(x,y,z) = k∇f=λ∇gandg(x,y,z)=k

Note: Evaluate fff at all solution points and compare to identify absolute max/min.

Practice

5 problems
  1. 1
    Find the maximum value of f(x,y)=3+2x−yf(x,y) = 3 + 2x - yf(x,y)=3+2x−y subject to the constraint x2+2xy+4y2=7x^2 + 2xy + 4y^2 = 7x2+2xy+4y2=7.
    no calculator, same as the exam
    Answer10answer recomputed · sympy
    1. The constraint g(x,y)=x2+2xy+4y2=7g(x,y)=x^2+2xy+4y^2=7g(x,y)=x2+2xy+4y2=7 is a closed curve (an ellipse), so fff attains a max and a min on it. Use Lagrange: ∇f=λ∇g\nabla f=\lambda\nabla g∇f=λ∇g.
    2. ∇f=⟨2, −1⟩\nabla f=\langle 2,\,-1\rangle∇f=⟨2,−1⟩ and ∇g=⟨2x+2y,  2x+8y⟩\nabla g=\langle 2x+2y,\;2x+8y\rangle∇g=⟨2x+2y,2x+8y⟩, so the system is 2=λ(2x+2y)2=\lambda(2x+2y)2=λ(2x+2y), −1=λ(2x+8y)-1=\lambda(2x+8y)−1=λ(2x+8y), x2+2xy+4y2=7x^2+2xy+4y^2=7x2+2xy+4y2=7.
    3. Add twice the second equation to the first to kill xxx: 2+2(−1)=λ[(2x+2y)+2(2x+8y)]2+2(-1)=\lambda\big[(2x+2y)+2(2x+8y)\big]2+2(−1)=λ[(2x+2y)+2(2x+8y)] gives 0=λ(6x+18y)0=\lambda(6x+18y)0=λ(6x+18y). Since λ≠0\lambda\ne 0λ=0 (else ∇f=0⃗\nabla f=\vec 0∇f=0, false), x=−3yx=-3yx=−3y.
    4. Substitute into the constraint: 9y2−6y2+4y2=7y2=79y^2-6y^2+4y^2=7y^2=79y2−6y2+4y2=7y2=7, so y=±1y=\pm 1y=±1 and (x,y)=(−3,1)(x,y)=(-3,1)(x,y)=(−3,1) or (3,−1)(3,-1)(3,−1).
    5. Evaluate: f(−3,1)=3−6−1=−4f(-3,1)=3-6-1=-4f(−3,1)=3−6−1=−4 and f(3,−1)=3+6+1=10f(3,-1)=3+6+1=10f(3,−1)=3+6+1=10.
    6. Maximum value =10=10=10 (attained at (3,−1)(3,-1)(3,−1); the minimum is −4-4−4).

    Trap∇g\nabla g∇g of the cross term is the usual casualty: ∂x(2xy)=2y\partial_x(2xy)=2y∂x​(2xy)=2y and ∂y(2xy)=2x\partial_y(2xy)=2x∂y​(2xy)=2x, so ∇g=⟨2x+2y, 2x+8y⟩\nabla g=\langle 2x+2y,\,2x+8y\rangle∇g=⟨2x+2y,2x+8y⟩, not ⟨2x+2y, 8y⟩\langle 2x+2y,\,8y\rangle⟨2x+2y,8y⟩. Also, Lagrange hands you *critical values*, plural. The largest of the list is the answer, so you must evaluate fff at every solution point, not just the first one you find.

  2. 2
    Find the maximum value of f(x,y)=8x−6yf(x,y) = 8x - 6yf(x,y)=8x−6y subject to the constraint (x−1)2+y2=1(x-1)^2 + y^2 = 1(x−1)2+y2=1.
    no calculator, same as the exam
    Answer18answer recomputed · sympy
    1. Constraint: the circle g(x,y)=(x−1)2+y2=1g(x,y)=(x-1)^2+y^2=1g(x,y)=(x−1)2+y2=1, centre (1,0)(1,0)(1,0), radius 111. fff is linear, so its extremes sit where the gradient of fff is normal to the circle.
    2. Lagrange: ⟨8,−6⟩=λ⟨2(x−1), 2y⟩\langle 8,-6\rangle=\lambda\langle 2(x-1),\,2y\rangle⟨8,−6⟩=λ⟨2(x−1),2y⟩, i.e. 8=2λ(x−1)8=2\lambda(x-1)8=2λ(x−1) and −6=2λy-6=2\lambda y−6=2λy.
    3. So x−1=4λx-1=\dfrac{4}{\lambda}x−1=λ4​ and y=−3λy=-\dfrac{3}{\lambda}y=−λ3​. Plug into the constraint: 16λ2+9λ2=1⇒λ2=25, λ=±5\dfrac{16}{\lambda^2}+\dfrac{9}{\lambda^2}=1\Rightarrow \lambda^2=25,\ \lambda=\pm 5λ216​+λ29​=1⇒λ2=25, λ=±5.
    4. λ=5\lambda=5λ=5: (x,y)=(95,−35)(x,y)=\left(\tfrac95,-\tfrac35\right)(x,y)=(59​,−53​), f=725+185=18f=\tfrac{72}{5}+\tfrac{18}{5}=18f=572​+518​=18. λ=−5\lambda=-5λ=−5: (x,y)=(15,35)(x,y)=\left(\tfrac15,\tfrac35\right)(x,y)=(51​,53​), f=85−185=−2f=\tfrac85-\tfrac{18}{5}=-2f=58​−518​=−2.
    5. Maximum value =18=18=18.
    6. Sanity check with geometry: f=8x−6yf=8x-6yf=8x−6y at the centre (1,0)(1,0)(1,0) is 888, and ∣∇f∣=64+36=10|\nabla f|=\sqrt{64+36}=10∣∇f∣=64+36​=10, so on a radius-111 circle fff ranges over 8±10={−2,18}8\pm 10=\{-2,18\}8±10={−2,18}. Same answer.

    TrapThe circle is not centred at the origin. Writing the constraint gradient as ⟨2x,2y⟩\langle 2x,2y\rangle⟨2x,2y⟩ (forgetting the shift) is the standard wreck here; it must be ⟨2(x−1), 2y⟩\langle 2(x-1),\,2y\rangle⟨2(x−1),2y⟩. The shortcut fmax⁡=f(centre)+∣∇f∣⋅Rf_{\max}=f(\text{centre})+|\nabla f|\cdot Rfmax​=f(centre)+∣∇f∣⋅R works only because fff is linear and the constraint is a circle; do not reach for it on an ellipse.

  3. 3
    The maximum and minimum values of f(x,y)=(x−2)2+(y−4)2f(x,y)=(x-2)^2+(y-4)^2f(x,y)=(x−2)2+(y−4)2 subject to x2+y2=5x^2+y^2=5x2+y2=5 are, respectively:
    no calculator, same as the exam
    AnswerMaximum 45, Minimum 5answer recomputed · sympy
    1. f(x,y)=(x−2)2+(y−4)2f(x,y)=(x-2)^2+(y-4)^2f(x,y)=(x−2)2+(y−4)2 is the squared distance from (2,4)(2,4)(2,4); the constraint is the circle of radius 5\sqrt55​ about the origin. So this is really a nearest/farthest point problem.
    2. Lagrange: ⟨2(x−2), 2(y−4)⟩=λ⟨2x, 2y⟩\langle 2(x-2),\,2(y-4)\rangle=\lambda\langle 2x,\,2y\rangle⟨2(x−2),2(y−4)⟩=λ⟨2x,2y⟩, i.e. x−2=λxx-2=\lambda xx−2=λx and y−4=λyy-4=\lambda yy−4=λy.
    3. Then x(1−λ)=2x(1-\lambda)=2x(1−λ)=2 and y(1−λ)=4y(1-\lambda)=4y(1−λ)=4, so y=2xy=2xy=2x (dividing; note λ≠1\lambda\ne1λ=1, since λ=1\lambda=1λ=1 would force 2=02=02=0).
    4. Constraint: x2+(2x)2=5x2=5⇒x=±1x^2+(2x)^2=5x^2=5\Rightarrow x=\pm1x2+(2x)2=5x2=5⇒x=±1, giving (1,2)(1,2)(1,2) and (−1,−2)(-1,-2)(−1,−2).
    5. f(1,2)=(1−2)2+(2−4)2=1+4=5f(1,2)=(1-2)^2+(2-4)^2=1+4=5f(1,2)=(1−2)2+(2−4)2=1+4=5. f(−1,−2)=(−3)2+(−6)2=9+36=45f(-1,-2)=(-3)^2+(-6)^2=9+36=45f(−1,−2)=(−3)2+(−6)2=9+36=45.
    6. Maximum 454545, minimum 555. (Check: ∣(2,4)∣=20=25|(2,4)|=\sqrt{20}=2\sqrt5∣(2,4)∣=20​=25​, so distances to the circle are 25∓52\sqrt5\mp\sqrt525​∓5​, whose squares are 555 and 454545.)

    TrapTwo traps. First, fff is the squared distance, so do not take a square root at the end and report 45\sqrt{45}45​ and 5\sqrt55​. Second, the point (2,4)(2,4)(2,4) lies *outside* the circle, so both critical points are genuine, one near and one far; the min is not 000.

  4. 4
    Find the maximum of f(x,y,z)=x+y+zf(x,y,z) = x+y+zf(x,y,z)=x+y+z subject to (x−1)2+y2+z2=1(x-1)^2+y^2+z^2=1(x−1)2+y2+z2=1.
    no calculator, same as the exam
    Answer1+31+\sqrt{3}1+3​answer recomputed · sympy

    2. System: 1=2λ(x−1)1=2\lambda(x-1)1=2λ(x−1), 1=2λy1=2\lambda y1=2λy, 1=2λz1=2\lambda z1=2λz. Hence x−1=y=z=12λx-1=y=z=\dfrac{1}{2\lambda}x−1=y=z=2λ1​.
    3. Substitute: 3(12λ)2=1⇒12λ=±133\left(\dfrac{1}{2\lambda}\right)^2=1\Rightarrow \dfrac{1}{2\lambda}=\pm\dfrac{1}{\sqrt3}3(2λ1​)2=1⇒2λ1​=±3​1​.
    4. Taking the +++ branch, x=1+13, y=z=13x=1+\tfrac{1}{\sqrt3},\ y=z=\tfrac{1}{\sqrt3}x=1+3​1​, y=z=3​1​, so f=1+33=1+3f=1+\tfrac{3}{\sqrt3}=1+\sqrt3f=1+3​3​=1+3​. The −-− branch gives 1−31-\sqrt31−3​.

    TrapSame shifted-centre trap as before: ∇g=⟨2(x−1),2y,2z⟩\nabla g=\langle 2(x-1),2y,2z\rangle∇g=⟨2(x−1),2y,2z⟩. And because the three partials give x−1=y=zx-1=y=zx−1=y=z (not x=y=zx=y=zx=y=z), the symmetric guess x=y=z=1/3x=y=z=1/\sqrt3x=y=z=1/3​ is wrong. The geometric check is f(centre)+∣∇f∣R=1+3⋅1f(\text{centre})+|\nabla f|R=1+\sqrt3\cdot1f(centre)+∣∇f∣R=1+3​⋅1.

  5. 5
    Find the absolute maximum value MMM and absolute minimum value mmm of f(x,y)=x+yf(x,y)=x+yf(x,y)=x+y subject to x2−xy+y2=1x^2-xy+y^2=1x2−xy+y2=1.
    no calculator, same as the exam
    AnswerM=2,  m=−2M=2,\;m=-2M=2,m=−2answer recomputed · sympy
    1. The constraint x2−xy+y2=1x^2-xy+y^2=1x2−xy+y2=1 is an ellipse (rotated 45∘45^\circ45∘), a closed bounded curve, so a max and a min both exist.
    2. Lagrange: ⟨1,1⟩=λ⟨2x−y,  2y−x⟩\langle1,1\rangle=\lambda\langle 2x-y,\;2y-x\rangle⟨1,1⟩=λ⟨2x−y,2y−x⟩, so 1=λ(2x−y)1=\lambda(2x-y)1=λ(2x−y) and 1=λ(2y−x)1=\lambda(2y-x)1=λ(2y−x).
    3. Setting the two right sides equal: 2x−y=2y−x⇒3x=3y⇒y=x2x-y=2y-x\Rightarrow 3x=3y\Rightarrow y=x2x−y=2y−x⇒3x=3y⇒y=x.
    4. Constraint: x2−x2+x2=x2=1x^2-x^2+x^2=x^2=1x2−x2+x2=x2=1, so (1,1)(1,1)(1,1) and (−1,−1)(-1,-1)(−1,−1).
    5. f(1,1)=2f(1,1)=2f(1,1)=2 and f(−1,−1)=−2f(-1,-1)=-2f(−1,−1)=−2, so M=2, m=−2\boxed{M=2,\ m=-2}M=2, m=−2​.

    TrapDifferentiating the cross term −xy-xy−xy: ∂x=−y\partial_x=-y∂x​=−y, ∂y=−x\partial_y=-x∂y​=−x — it is easy to drop a sign and get 2x+y2x+y2x+y. Also, cancelling λ\lambdaλ from the two equations is legal here only because λ≠0\lambda\ne0λ=0 (if λ=0\lambda=0λ=0 then 1=01=01=0), so you should say so rather than divide blindly.

02

Double Integrals over Rectangular Regions

Lesson 18 · §16.1
Don't know this yet? §s161 in the full guide →
From the official study guide

Double Integral over a Rectangle

For R=[a,b]×[c,d]R = [a,b] \times [c,d]R=[a,b]×[c,d]:

∬Rf(x,y) dA=∫ab∫cdf(x,y) dy dx=∫cd∫abf(x,y) dx dy\iint_R f(x,y)\,dA = \int_a^b \int_c^d f(x,y)\,dy\,dx = \int_c^d \int_a^b f(x,y)\,dx\,dy∬R​f(x,y)dA=∫ab​∫cd​f(x,y)dydx=∫cd​∫ab​f(x,y)dxdy

Fubini's Theorem

If fff is continuous on R=[a,b]×[c,d]R = [a,b]\times[c,d]R=[a,b]×[c,d], the order of integration may be switched:

∫ab∫cdf(x,y) dy dx=∫cd∫abf(x,y) dx dy\int_a^b\int_c^d f(x,y)\,dy\,dx = \int_c^d\int_a^b f(x,y)\,dx\,dy∫ab​∫cd​f(x,y)dydx=∫cd​∫ab​f(x,y)dxdy

Riemann Sum Definition

Partition [a,b][a,b][a,b] into mmm subintervals and [c,d][c,d][c,d] into nnn subintervals, each of width Δx=b−am\Delta x = \frac{b-a}{m}Δx=mb−a​ and Δy=d−cn\Delta y = \frac{d-c}{n}Δy=nd−c​. Choose sample points (xij∗,yij∗)(x_{ij}^*, y_{ij}^*)(xij∗​,yij∗​) in each subrectangle RijR_{ij}Rij​:

∬Rf(x,y) dA=lim⁡m,n→∞∑i=1m∑j=1nf(xij∗, yij∗) ΔA\iint_R f(x,y)\,dA = \lim_{m,n\to\infty}\sum_{i=1}^{m}\sum_{j=1}^{n} f(x_{ij}^*,\, y_{ij}^*)\,\Delta A∬R​f(x,y)dA=m,n→∞lim​i=1∑m​j=1∑n​f(xij∗​,yij∗​)ΔA

where ΔA=Δx Δy\Delta A = \Delta x\,\Delta yΔA=ΔxΔy is the area of each subrectangle.

  • Using midpoints: xi∗=xi−1+xi2x_i^* = \frac{x_{i-1}+x_i}{2}xi∗​=2xi−1​+xi​​, yj∗=yj−1+yj2y_j^* = \frac{y_{j-1}+y_j}{2}yj∗​=2yj−1​+yj​​
  • The double integral gives the signed volume between the surface z=f(x,y)z = f(x,y)z=f(x,y) and the xyxyxy-plane

Practice

5 problems
  1. 1
    Compute ∫01∫04xy dx dy\displaystyle\int_0^1\int_0^4 \sqrt{xy}\,dx\,dy∫01​∫04​xy​dxdy.
    no calculator, same as the exam
    Answer329\tfrac{32}{9}932​answer recomputed · sympy
    1. The integrand factors, xy=x y\sqrt{xy}=\sqrt{x}\,\sqrt{y}xy​=x​y​, and the region is the rectangle [0,4]×[0,1][0,4]\times[0,1][0,4]×[0,1], so the double integral splits into a product of single integrals.
    2. ∫01 ⁣ ⁣∫04xy dx dy=(∫04x dx)(∫01y dy)\displaystyle\int_0^1\!\!\int_0^4\sqrt{x}\sqrt{y}\,dx\,dy=\left(\int_0^4\sqrt{x}\,dx\right)\left(\int_0^1\sqrt{y}\,dy\right)∫01​∫04​x​y​dxdy=(∫04​x​dx)(∫01​y​dy).
    3. ∫04x1/2dx=23x3/2∣04=23⋅8=163\displaystyle\int_0^4 x^{1/2}dx=\tfrac23 x^{3/2}\Big|_0^4=\tfrac23\cdot 8=\tfrac{16}{3}∫04​x1/2dx=32​x3/2​04​=32​⋅8=316​.
    4. ∫01y1/2dy=23\displaystyle\int_0^1 y^{1/2}dy=\tfrac23∫01​y1/2dy=32​.
    5. Product: 163⋅23=329\dfrac{16}{3}\cdot\dfrac23=\dfrac{32}{9}316​⋅32​=932​.

    TrapRead the differentials: dx dydx\,dydxdy means the inner variable is xxx (limits 000 to 444) and the outer is yyy (limits 000 to 111). Pairing xxx with [0,1][0,1][0,1] gives 23⋅163\tfrac23\cdot\tfrac{16}{3}32​⋅316​ by luck here, but on a non-symmetric integrand the same misreading is fatal. The split into a product is legal only because the integrand factors and the limits are constants.

Double Integrals over General Regions

Lesson 19 · §16.2

From the official study guide

Type I Region (vertical strips)

Region bounded by functions of xxx: g1(x)≤y≤g2(x)g_1(x) \le y \le g_2(x)g1​(x)≤y≤g2​(x), a≤x≤ba \le x \le ba≤x≤b

∬Df(x,y) dA=∫ab∫g1(x)g2(x)f(x,y) dy dx\iint_D f(x,y)\,dA = \int_a^b\int_{g_1(x)}^{g_2(x)} f(x,y)\,dy\,dx∬D​f(x,y)dA=∫ab​∫g1​(x)g2​(x)​f(x,y)dydx

Type II Region (horizontal strips)

Region bounded by functions of yyy: h1(y)≤x≤h2(y)h_1(y) \le x \le h_2(y)h1​(y)≤x≤h2​(y), c≤y≤dc \le y \le dc≤y≤d

∬Df(x,y) dA=∫cd∫h1(y)h2(y)f(x,y) dx dy\iint_D f(x,y)\,dA = \int_c^d\int_{h_1(y)}^{h_2(y)} f(x,y)\,dx\,dy∬D​f(x,y)dA=∫cd​∫h1​(y)h2​(y)​f(x,y)dxdy

Reversing Order of Integration

Sketch the region, identify bounds for the opposite order, then re-write the integral. This is often necessary when the inner integral has no elementary antiderivative.

04

Double Integrals in Polar Coordinates

Lesson 20 · §16.3
Don't know this yet? §s163 in the full guide →
From the official study guide

Polar Coordinate Substitution

Use x=rcos⁡θx = r\cos\thetax=rcosθ, y=rsin⁡θy = r\sin\thetay=rsinθ, x2+y2=r2x^2+y^2=r^2x2+y2=r2:

∬Df(x,y) dA=∫αβ∫r1(θ)r2(θ)f(rcos⁡θ, rsin⁡θ) r dr dθ\iint_D f(x,y)\,dA = \int_\alpha^\beta\int_{r_1(\theta)}^{r_2(\theta)} f(r\cos\theta,\, r\sin\theta)\,r\,dr\,d\theta∬D​f(x,y)dA=∫αβ​∫r1​(θ)r2​(θ)​f(rcosθ,rsinθ)rdrdθ

Key: Don't forget the Jacobian factor rrr in dA=r dr dθdA = r\,dr\,d\thetadA=rdrdθ.

When to Use Polar Coordinates

  • Region is a disk, annulus, or sector
  • Integrand contains x2+y2x^2 + y^2x2+y2
  • Region has circular symmetry

Practice

5 problems
  1. 1

    no calculator, same as the exam
    Answer9π2\tfrac{9\pi}{2}29π​answer recomputed · sympy
    1. Identify the region: 0≤x≤30\le x\le30≤x≤3 and 0≤y≤9−x20\le y\le\sqrt{9-x^2}0≤y≤9−x2​, i.e. x2+y2≤9x^2+y^2\le9x2+y2≤9 with x,y≥0x,y\ge0x,y≥0 — the quarter disk of radius 333 in the first quadrant.
    2. Polar: x=rcos⁡θx=r\cos\thetax=rcosθ, y=rsin⁡θy=r\sin\thetay=rsinθ, x2+y2=r\sqrt{x^2+y^2}=rx2+y2​=r, and dA=r dr dθdA=r\,dr\,d\thetadA=rdrdθ. The region is 0≤r≤30\le r\le30≤r≤3, 0≤θ≤π20\le\theta\le\dfrac{\pi}{2}0≤θ≤2π​.
    3. ∫03 ⁣ ⁣∫09−x2x2+y2 dy dx=∫0π/2 ⁣ ⁣∫03r⋅r dr dθ=∫0π/2 ⁣ ⁣∫03r2 dr dθ\displaystyle\int_0^3\!\!\int_0^{\sqrt{9-x^2}}\sqrt{x^2+y^2}\,dy\,dx=\int_0^{\pi/2}\!\!\int_0^3 r\cdot r\,dr\,d\theta=\int_0^{\pi/2}\!\!\int_0^3 r^2\,dr\,d\theta∫03​∫09−x2​​x2+y2​dydx=∫0π/2​∫03​r⋅rdrdθ=∫0π/2​∫03​r2drdθ.
    4. Inner: r33∣03=9\dfrac{r^3}{3}\Big|_0^3=93r3​​03​=9.
    5. Outer: 9⋅π2=9π29\cdot\dfrac{\pi}{2}=\dfrac{9\pi}{2}9⋅2π​=29π​.

    TrapThe integrand becomes r2r^2r2, not rrr: one factor of rrr is x2+y2\sqrt{x^2+y^2}x2+y2​ and the second is the Jacobian from dA=r dr dθdA=r\,dr\,d\thetadA=rdrdθ. Dropping the Jacobian gives 9π4\tfrac{9\pi}{4}49π​. Second trap: θ\thetaθ runs only to π/2\pi/2π/2 — the limits x∈[0,3]x\in[0,3]x∈[0,3], y≥0y\ge0y≥0 give a quarter disk, not a half disk.

From the official study guide

Iterated Triple Integral

∭Ef(x,y,z) dV=∫ab∫g1(x)g2(x)∫u1(x,y)u2(x,y)f(x,y,z) dz dy dx\iiint_E f(x,y,z)\,dV = \int_a^b\int_{g_1(x)}^{g_2(x)}\int_{u_1(x,y)}^{u_2(x,y)} f(x,y,z)\,dz\,dy\,dx∭E​f(x,y,z)dV=∫ab​∫g1​(x)g2​(x)​∫u1​(x,y)u2​(x,y)​f(x,y,z)dzdydx

Applications

  • Volume: V=∭EdVV = \displaystyle\iiint_E dVV=∭E​dV
  • Average value: fˉ=1V∭Ef dV\bar{f} = \dfrac{1}{V}\displaystyle\iiint_E f\,dVfˉ​=V1​∭E​fdV

Note: There are 6 possible orders of integration — choose the order that fits the region and integrand most naturally.

Practice

5 problems
  1. 1
    Evaluate ∫01 ⁣∫01 ⁣∫02−yex dz dx dy\displaystyle\int_0^1\!\int_0^1\!\int_0^{2-y} e^x\,dz\,dx\,dy∫01​∫01​∫02−y​exdzdxdy.
    no calculator, same as the exam
    Answer32(e−1)\tfrac{3}{2}(e-1)23​(e−1)answer recomputed · sympy
    1. Read the order off the differentials: dz dx dydz\,dx\,dydzdxdy. The innermost variable is zzz, and the integrand exe^xex does not contain zzz — so the inner integral is just multiplication by the height.
    2. ∫02−yex dz=ex (2−y)\displaystyle\int_0^{2-y}e^x\,dz=e^x\,(2-y)∫02−y​exdz=ex(2−y).
    3. Now the xxx and yyy limits are both constants, and what is left separates: ∫01 ⁣∫01ex(2−y) dx dy=(∫01ex dx)(∫01(2−y) dy)\displaystyle\int_0^1\!\int_0^1 e^x(2-y)\,dx\,dy=\left(\int_0^1 e^x\,dx\right)\left(\int_0^1(2-y)\,dy\right)∫01​∫01​ex(2−y)dxdy=(∫01​exdx)(∫01​(2−y)dy).
    4. ∫01ex dx=e−1\displaystyle\int_0^1 e^x\,dx=e-1∫01​exdx=e−1 and ∫01(2−y) dy=2−12=32\displaystyle\int_0^1(2-y)\,dy=2-\tfrac12=\tfrac32∫01​(2−y)dy=2−21​=23​.
    5. Product: 32(e−1)\tfrac{3}{2}(e-1)23​(e−1).

    TrapThe limit 2−y2-y2−y sits on the inner integral while yyy is the outer variable. That is legal — inner limits may involve any variable integrated later — but it means you cannot do the yyy-integral first. Someone who starts at the outside gets ∫01(2−y) dy\int_0^1(2-y)\,dy∫01​(2−y)dy sitting where a zzz-integral belongs and loses the factor entirely.

    4. For a fixed xxx, yyy runs from 000 up to that line: b=4−2xb=4-2xb=4−2x.

  3. 3
    Let DDD be the solid bounded by x=0x=0x=0, z=0z=0z=0, y=xy=xy=x, and x+y+z=2x+y+z=2x+y+z=2. Write ∭Df dV\iiint_D f\,dV∭D​fdV as an iterated integral.

    1. Four surfaces, so list the inequalities: x≥0x\ge0x≥0, z≥0z\ge0z≥0, y≥xy\ge xy≥x, and x+y+z≤2x+y+z\le2x+y+z≤2.

    6. Those two limits cross when 2−x−z=x2-x-z=x2−x−z=x, i.e. at z=2−2xz=2-2xz=2−2x — so zzz must stop at 2−2x2-2x2−2x, giving ∫01 ⁣∫02−2x ⁣∫x2−x−zf dy dz dx\displaystyle\int_0^1\!\int_0^{2-2x}\!\int_x^{2-x-z}f\,dy\,dz\,dx∫01​∫02−2x​∫x2−x−z​fdydzdx.

Writing zzz from 000 to 2−x2-x2−x (the plane's zzz-intercept above y=0y=0y=0) puts zzz in a range where the inner yyy-limits are upside-down, 2−x−z<x2-x-z<x2−x−z<x, and the integral quietly subtracts the phantom slab instead of erroring.

    The official answer is wrongThe second offered order is wrong as printed. With zzz running to 2−x2-x2−x, every z>2−2xz>2-2xz>2−2x has 2−x−z<x2-x-z<x2−x−z<x, so the inner yyy-integral runs backwards. 06

Triple Integrals in Cylindrical Coordinates

Lesson 22 · §16.5
Don't know this yet? §s165c in the full guide →
From the official study guide

Cylindrical Coordinates

Relation to rectangular coordinates:

x=rcos⁡θ,y=rsin⁡θ,z=zx = r\cos\theta,\quad y = r\sin\theta,\quad z = zx=rcosθ,y=rsinθ,z=z r2=x2+y2,tan⁡θ=yxr^2 = x^2+y^2,\quad \tan\theta = \frac{y}{x}r2=x2+y2,tanθ=xy​

Triple Integral in Cylindrical Coordinates

∭Ef(x,y,z) dV=∫αβ∫r1r2∫u1u2f(rcos⁡θ,rsin⁡θ,z) r dz dr dθ\iiint_E f(x,y,z)\,dV = \int_\alpha^\beta\int_{r_1}^{r_2}\int_{u_1}^{u_2} f(r\cos\theta,r\sin\theta,z)\,r\,dz\,dr\,d\theta∭E​f(x,y,z)dV=∫αβ​∫r1​r2​​∫u1​u2​​f(rcosθ,rsinθ,z)rdzdrdθ

Key: Don't forget the Jacobian factor rrr in dV=r dz dr dθdV = r\,dz\,dr\,d\thetadV=rdzdrdθ.

When to Use Cylindrical Coordinates

  • Region has an axis of symmetry along the zzz-axis
  • Integrand or region involves x2+y2x^2 + y^2x2+y2
  • Region is bounded by a cylinder x2+y2=a2x^2+y^2 = a^2x2+y2=a2, cone, or paraboloid

  5. 5
    Write the volume of the solid bounded by the cone z2=x2+y2z^2=x^2+y^2z2=x2+y2 between the planes z=1z=1z=1 and z=2z=2z=2 as a spherical-coordinates integral.

    Answer∫02π ⁣∫0π/4 ⁣∫sec⁡ϕ2sec⁡ϕρ2sin⁡ϕ dρ dϕ dθ\displaystyle\int_0^{2\pi}\!\int_0^{\pi/4}\!\int_{\sec\phi}^{2\sec\phi}\rho^2\sin\phi\,d\rho\,d\phi\,d\theta∫02π​∫0π/4​∫secϕ2secϕ​ρ2sinϕdρdϕdθanswer recomputed · sympy
    1. In spherical, the cone z2=x2+y2z^2=x^2+y^2z2=x2+y2 with z>0z>0z>0 is the single surface ϕ=π4\phi=\frac{\pi}{4}ϕ=4π​, and the solid inside it is 0≤ϕ≤π40\le\phi\le\frac{\pi}{4}0≤ϕ≤4π​.
    2. A horizontal plane is not a constant in spherical: z=ρcos⁡ϕz=\rho\cos\phiz=ρcosϕ, so z=1z=1z=1 becomes ρ=sec⁡ϕ\rho=\sec\phiρ=secϕ and z=2z=2z=2 becomes ρ=2sec⁡ϕ\rho=2\sec\phiρ=2secϕ.
    3. Those are the ρ\rhoρ-limits, and they depend on ϕ\phiϕ — so ρ\rhoρ must be integrated first.
    4. dV=ρ2sin⁡ϕ dρ dϕ dθdV=\rho^2\sin\phi\,d\rho\,d\phi\,d\thetadV=ρ2sinϕdρdϕdθ, full revolution in θ\thetaθ:
    5. V=∫02π ⁣∫0π/4 ⁣∫sec⁡ϕ2sec⁡ϕρ2sin⁡ϕ dρ dϕ dθ\displaystyle V=\int_0^{2\pi}\!\int_0^{\pi/4}\!\int_{\sec\phi}^{2\sec\phi}\rho^2\sin\phi\,d\rho\,d\phi\,d\thetaV=∫02π​∫0π/4​∫secϕ2secϕ​ρ2sinϕdρdϕdθ.
    6. Worth confirming in cylindrical, where it is a stack of disks of radius zzz: ∫02π ⁣∫12 ⁣∫0zr dr dz dθ=∫12πz2 dz=7π3\displaystyle\int_0^{2\pi}\!\int_1^2\!\int_0^{z}r\,dr\,dz\,d\theta=\int_1^2\pi z^2\,dz=\frac{7\pi}{3}∫02π​∫12​∫0z​rdrdzdθ=∫12​πz2dz=37π​ — and the spherical integral gives the same.

    TrapWriting the planes as constant ρ\rhoρ (say ρ\rhoρ from 111 to 222), which describes the region between two spheres, not two planes — that is a spherical shell wedge, volume 2π3(8−1)(1−cos⁡π4)\frac{2\pi}{3}(8-1)(1-\cos\frac\pi4)32π​(8−1)(1−cos4π​), not 7π3\frac{7\pi}{3}37π​. Any flat boundary not through the origin becomes ρ=(something)sec⁡ϕ\rho=\text{(something)}\sec\phiρ=(something)secϕ and forces dρd\rhodρ innermost.

07

Triple Integrals in Spherical Coordinates

Lesson 23 · §16.5
Don't know this yet? §s165s in the full guide →
From the official study guide

Spherical Coordinates

x=ρsin⁡ϕcos⁡θ,y=ρsin⁡ϕsin⁡θ,z=ρcos⁡ϕx = \rho\sin\phi\cos\theta,\quad y = \rho\sin\phi\sin\theta,\quad z = \rho\cos\phix=ρsinϕcosθ,y=ρsinϕsinθ,z=ρcosϕ ρ2=x2+y2+z2,ρ≥0,0≤ϕ≤π,0≤θ≤2π\rho^2 = x^2+y^2+z^2, \quad \rho \ge 0,\quad 0 \le \phi \le \pi,\quad 0 \le \theta \le 2\piρ2=x2+y2+z2,ρ≥0,0≤ϕ≤π,0≤θ≤2π

Triple Integral in Spherical Coordinates

∭Ef dV=∫02π∫0ϕmax⁡∫0ρmax⁡f ρ2sin⁡ϕ dρ dϕ dθ\iiint_E f\,dV = \int_0^{2\pi}\int_0^{\phi_{\max}}\int_0^{\rho_{\max}} f\,\rho^2\sin\phi\,d\rho\,d\phi\,d\theta∭E​fdV=∫02π​∫0ϕmax​​∫0ρmax​​fρ2sinϕdρdϕdθ

Key: The Jacobian is ρ2sin⁡ϕ\rho^2\sin\phiρ2sinϕ. Don't forget it!

Useful Identities

  • Sphere: ρ=a\rho = aρ=a
  • Cone: ϕ=ϕ0\phi = \phi_0ϕ=ϕ0​ (half-angle from positive zzz-axis)
  • z=ρcos⁡ϕz = \rho\cos\phiz=ρcosϕ,   r=ρsin⁡ϕ\;r = \rho\sin\phir=ρsinϕ

    3. The cone z=3x2+3y2=3 x2+y2z=\sqrt{3x^2+3y^2}=\sqrt3\,\sqrt{x^2+y^2}z=3x2+3y2​=3​x2+y2​ has tan⁡ϕ=x2+y2z=13\tan\phi=\dfrac{\sqrt{x^2+y^2}}{z}=\dfrac{1}{\sqrt3}tanϕ=zx2+y2​​=3​1​.
    4. So ϕ=π6\phi=\frac{\pi}{6}ϕ=6π​, and 'inside the cone' means 0≤ϕ≤π60\le\phi\le\frac{\pi}{6}0≤ϕ≤6π​: a=π6a=\frac{\pi}{6}a=6π​.
    5. V=∫02π ⁣∫0π/6 ⁣∫02ρ2sin⁡ϕ dρ dϕ dθ\displaystyle V=\int_0^{2\pi}\!\int_0^{\pi/6}\!\int_0^{2}\rho^2\sin\phi\,d\rho\,d\phi\,d\thetaV=∫02π​∫0π/6​∫02​ρ2sinϕdρdϕdθ.

Taking tan⁡ϕ=3\tan\phi=\sqrt3tanϕ=3​ gives ϕ=π3\phi=\frac{\pi}{3}ϕ=3π​, which is the complementary wedge and roughly four times the volume. Second trap: writing c=ρsin⁡ϕc=\rho\sin\phic=ρsinϕ, the *polar* Jacobian with a ρ\rhoρ in it, which is dimensionally wrong for a volume.

Integrals in Mass Calculations

Lesson 24 · §16.6
Don't know this yet? §s166 in the full guide →
From the official study guide

Mass, Moments, and Center of Mass

For a lamina (2D) with density δ(x,y)\delta(x,y)δ(x,y):

m=∬Dδ(x,y) dAm = \iint_D \delta(x,y)\,dAm=∬D​δ(x,y)dA xˉ=1m∬Dx δ(x,y) dA,yˉ=1m∬Dy δ(x,y) dA\bar{x} = \frac{1}{m}\iint_D x\,\delta(x,y)\,dA, \qquad \bar{y} = \frac{1}{m}\iint_D y\,\delta(x,y)\,dAxˉ=m1​∬D​xδ(x,y)dA,yˉ​=m1​∬D​yδ(x,y)dA

3D Solid

For a solid EEE with density δ(x,y,z)\delta(x,y,z)δ(x,y,z):

m=∭Eδ(x,y,z) dVm = \iiint_E \delta(x,y,z)\,dVm=∭E​δ(x,y,z)dV xˉ=1m∭Ex δ dV,yˉ=1m∭Ey δ dV,zˉ=1m∭Ez δ dV\bar{x} = \frac{1}{m}\iiint_E x\,\delta\,dV,\quad \bar{y} = \frac{1}{m}\iiint_E y\,\delta\,dV,\quad \bar{z} = \frac{1}{m}\iiint_E z\,\delta\,dVxˉ=m1​∭E​xδdV,yˉ​=m1​∭E​yδdV,zˉ=m1​∭E​zδdV

Moments of Inertia

Ix=∬Dy2 δ dA,Iy=∬Dx2 δ dA,I0=∬D(x2+y2) δ dAI_x = \iint_D y^2\,\delta\,dA,\quad I_y = \iint_D x^2\,\delta\,dA,\quad I_0 = \iint_D (x^2+y^2)\,\delta\,dAIx​=∬D​y2δdA,Iy​=∬D​x2δdA,I0​=∬D​(x2+y2)δdA

09

Vector Fields

Lesson 25 · §17.1
Don't know this yet? §s171 in the full guide →
From the official study guide

Definition

A vector field assigns a vector to each point in a region:

F⃗(x,y)=P(x,y) i⃗+Q(x,y) j⃗=⟨P,Q⟩\vec{F}(x,y) = P(x,y)\,\vec{i} + Q(x,y)\,\vec{j} = \langle P, Q \rangleF(x,y)=P(x,y)i+Q(x,y)j​=⟨P,Q⟩ F⃗(x,y,z)=P i⃗+Q j⃗+R k⃗=⟨P,Q,R⟩\vec{F}(x,y,z) = P\,\vec{i} + Q\,\vec{j} + R\,\vec{k} = \langle P, Q, R \rangleF(x,y,z)=Pi+Qj​+Rk=⟨P,Q,R⟩

Conservative Vector Fields

A vector field F⃗\vec{F}F is conservative if there exists a scalar function fff (the potential function) such that:

F⃗=∇f⟺P=fx,  Q=fy  (and R=fz)\vec{F} = \nabla f \qquad \Longleftrightarrow \qquad P = f_x,\; Q = f_y \; (\text{and }R = f_z)F=∇f⟺P=fx​,Q=fy​(and R=fz​)

Test for Conservative Field in 2D

F⃗=⟨P,Q⟩ is conservative  ⟺  ∂P∂y=∂Q∂x\vec{F} = \langle P, Q \rangle \text{ is conservative} \iff \frac{\partial P}{\partial y} = \frac{\partial Q}{\partial x}F=⟨P,Q⟩ is conservative⟺∂y∂P​=∂x∂Q​

Practice

4 problems
  1. 1
    Consider F⃗=⟨eyz−ysin⁡(xy),  zxeyz−xsin⁡(xy),  xyeyz⟩\vec{F}=\langle e^{yz}-y\sin(xy),\;zxe^{yz}-x\sin(xy),\;xye^{yz}\rangleF=⟨eyz−ysin(xy),zxeyz−xsin(xy),xyeyz⟩. Find a potential function φ\varphiφ if one exists.
    no calculator, same as the exam
    Answerxeyz+cos⁡(xy)xe^{yz}+\cos(xy)xeyz+cos(xy)answer recomputed · sympy
    1. We want φ\varphiφ with ∇φ=F⃗\nabla\varphi=\vec F∇φ=F, so start with the component that is easiest to antidifferentiate and then patch it up.
    2. Integrate the first component in xxx, holding y,zy,zy,z fixed: φ=∫(eyz−ysin⁡(xy)) dx=xeyz+cos⁡(xy)+g(y,z)\varphi=\displaystyle\int\big(e^{yz}-y\sin(xy)\big)\,dx = xe^{yz}+\cos(xy)+g(y,z)φ=∫(eyz−ysin(xy))dx=xeyz+cos(xy)+g(y,z).
    3. The sign is the whole game here: ddxcos⁡(xy)=−ysin⁡(xy)\dfrac{d}{dx}\cos(xy)=-y\sin(xy)dxd​cos(xy)=−ysin(xy), so the antiderivative of −ysin⁡(xy)-y\sin(xy)−ysin(xy) is +cos⁡(xy)+\cos(xy)+cos(xy).
    4. Now differentiate that candidate in yyy: φy=xzeyz−xsin⁡(xy)+gy\varphi_y = xze^{yz}-x\sin(xy)+g_yφy​=xzeyz−xsin(xy)+gy​.
    5. Compare with the given second component zxeyz−xsin⁡(xy)zxe^{yz}-x\sin(xy)zxeyz−xsin(xy): they already match, so gy=0g_y=0gy​=0.
    6. Differentiate in zzz: φz=xyeyz+gz\varphi_z = xye^{yz}+g_zφz​=xyeyz+gz​, and the third component is xyeyzxye^{yz}xyeyz, so gz=0g_z=0gz​=0 too. Hence ggg is a constant.
    7. φ=xeyz+cos⁡(xy)\varphi = xe^{yz}+\cos(xy)φ=xeyz+cos(xy) (any additive constant is also a potential).

    TrapWriting ∫−ysin⁡(xy) dx=−cos⁡(xy)\int -y\sin(xy)\,dx = -\cos(xy)∫−ysin(xy)dx=−cos(xy). The −y-y−y out front is exactly the inner derivative, so the two minus signs cancel and you get +cos⁡(xy)+\cos(xy)+cos(xy). Getting this backwards still passes a careless φx\varphi_xφx​ check if you also flip the sign when differentiating.

  2. 2
    Let a≠0a\ne0a=0 and CCC be the curve x2−2y2=ax^2-2y^2=ax2−2y2=a. Which F⃗\vec{F}F is orthogonal to the tangent of CCC at every point (x0,y0)(x_0,y_0)(x0​,y0​) on CCC?
    no calculator, same as the exam
    Answer⟨2x,−4y⟩\langle 2x,-4y\rangle⟨2x,−4y⟩answer recomputed · sympy
    1. CCC is the level curve g(x,y)=ag(x,y)=ag(x,y)=a of g(x,y)=x2−2y2g(x,y)=x^2-2y^2g(x,y)=x2−2y2.
    2. Key fact: the gradient of ggg is normal to every level curve of ggg, hence orthogonal to the tangent of CCC at each point.
    3. ∇g=⟨gx,gy⟩=⟨2x, −4y⟩\nabla g=\langle g_x,g_y\rangle = \langle 2x,\,-4y\rangle∇g=⟨gx​,gy​⟩=⟨2x,−4y⟩.
    4. So F⃗=⟨2x,−4y⟩\vec F=\langle 2x,-4y\rangleF=⟨2x,−4y⟩ is orthogonal to T⃗\vec TT at every (x0,y0)(x_0,y_0)(x0​,y0​) on CCC (and so is any scalar multiple of it).
    5. Sanity check by hand: implicit differentiation of x2−2y2=ax^2-2y^2=ax2−2y2=a gives 2x−4y y′=02x-4y\,y'=02x−4yy′=0, so T⃗∥⟨4y,2x⟩\vec T\parallel\langle 4y,2x\rangleT∥⟨4y,2x⟩, and ⟨2x,−4y⟩⋅⟨4y,2x⟩=8xy−8xy=0\langle 2x,-4y\rangle\cdot\langle 4y,2x\rangle = 8xy-8xy=0⟨2x,−4y⟩⋅⟨4y,2x⟩=8xy−8xy=0.

    TrapDropping the minus sign and answering ⟨2x,4y⟩\langle 2x,4y\rangle⟨2x,4y⟩ — that is ∇(x2+2y2)\nabla(x^2+2y^2)∇(x2+2y2), the normal to an ellipse, not to this hyperbola. The other classic miss is handing back the tangent ⟨4y,2x⟩\langle 4y,2x\rangle⟨4y,2x⟩ instead of the normal.

  3. 3
    Which vector field corresponds to the field with vectors rotating counterclockwise (pointing left above the xxx-axis, right below it)?
    no calculator, same as the exam
    Answer⟨−y,x⟩\langle -y,x\rangle⟨−y,x⟩answer recomputed · sympy
    1. Counterclockwise rotation means the field is tangent to circles centered at the origin, pointing in the direction of increasing angle.
    2. Parametrize a circle the counterclockwise way: r⃗(t)=⟨cos⁡t,sin⁡t⟩\vec r(t)=\langle\cos t,\sin t\rangler(t)=⟨cost,sint⟩.
    3. The direction of travel is r⃗ ′(t)=⟨−sin⁡t,cos⁡t⟩\vec r\,{}'(t)=\langle-\sin t,\cos t\rangler′(t)=⟨−sint,cost⟩.
    4. Rewrite that at the point itself, using x=cos⁡tx=\cos tx=cost, y=sin⁡ty=\sin ty=sint: the tangent direction is ⟨−y, x⟩\langle -y,\,x\rangle⟨−y,x⟩.
    5. Spot-check the description: above the xxx-axis take (0,1)(0,1)(0,1), giving ⟨−1,0⟩\langle-1,0\rangle⟨−1,0⟩ (points left); below take (0,−1)(0,-1)(0,−1), giving ⟨1,0⟩\langle1,0\rangle⟨1,0⟩ (points right). Matches.
    6. F⃗=⟨−y, x⟩\vec F=\langle -y,\,x\rangleF=⟨−y,x⟩.

    TrapAnswering ⟨y,−x⟩\langle y,-x\rangle⟨y,−x⟩, which is the same picture run clockwise. Always test one concrete point above the xxx-axis rather than trusting the sign pattern; ⟨y,−x⟩\langle y,-x\rangle⟨y,−x⟩ gives ⟨1,0⟩\langle1,0\rangle⟨1,0⟩ at (0,1)(0,1)(0,1), pointing right, which is the wrong rotation.

  4. 4
    Suppose f(x,y,z)=xy2z3f(x,y,z)=xy^2z^3f(x,y,z)=xy2z3. Find div⁡(∇f)\operatorname{div}(\nabla f)div(∇f) at the point (2,−1,1)(2,-1,1)(2,−1,1).

    Answer16answer recomputed · sympy

    2. ∇f=⟨y2z3,  2xyz3,  3xy2z2⟩\nabla f=\langle y^2z^3,\;2xyz^3,\;3xy^2z^2\rangle∇f=⟨y2z3,2xyz3,3xy2z2⟩.
    3. Take the matching partial of each component: fxx=∂x(y2z3)=0f_{xx}=\partial_x(y^2z^3)=0fxx​=∂x​(y2z3)=0, fyy=∂y(2xyz3)=2xz3f_{yy}=\partial_y(2xyz^3)=2xz^3fyy​=∂y​(2xyz3)=2xz3, fzz=∂z(3xy2z2)=6xy2zf_{zz}=\partial_z(3xy^2z^2)=6xy^2zfzz​=∂z​(3xy2z2)=6xy2z.

First, differentiating the wrong slot — you must take ∂x\partial_x∂x​ of the first component, ∂y\partial_y∂y​ of the second, ∂z\partial_z∂z​ of the third, not all three of one component. Second, (−1)2=+1(-1)^2=+1(−1)2=+1: plugging y=−1y=-1y=−1 into 6xy2z6xy^2z6xy2z gives +12+12+12, and writing −12-12−12 turns 161616 into −8-8−8.

From the official study guide

Line Integral of a Scalar Function

For curve CCC parametrized by r⃗(t)\vec{r}(t)r(t), a≤t≤ba \le t \le ba≤t≤b:

∫Cf(x,y,z) ds=∫abf(r⃗(t)) ∣r⃗′(t)∣ dt\int_C f(x,y,z)\,ds = \int_a^b f(\vec{r}(t))\,|\vec{r}'(t)|\,dt∫C​f(x,y,z)ds=∫ab​f(r(t))∣r′(t)∣dt

Interpretations

  • Arc length: ∫Cds=∫ab∣r⃗′(t)∣ dt\displaystyle\int_C ds = \int_a^b |\vec{r}'(t)|\,dt∫C​ds=∫ab​∣r′(t)∣dt
  • Mass of a wire with linear density δ\deltaδ: m=∫Cδ dsm = \displaystyle\int_C \delta\,dsm=∫C​δds

Practice

5 problems

Line Integrals of Vector Fields

Lesson 27 · §17.2

From the official study guide

Line Integral of a Vector Field (Work)

The work done by F⃗\vec{F}F along curve CCC:

∫CF⃗⋅dr⃗=∫abF⃗(r⃗(t))⋅r⃗′(t) dt=∫CP dx+Q dy+R dz\int_C \vec{F}\cdot d\vec{r} = \int_a^b \vec{F}(\vec{r}(t))\cdot\vec{r}'(t)\,dt = \int_C P\,dx + Q\,dy + R\,dz∫C​F⋅dr=∫ab​F(r(t))⋅r′(t)dt=∫C​Pdx+Qdy+Rdz

Key Properties

  • Reversing orientation changes the sign: ∫−CF⃗⋅dr⃗=−∫CF⃗⋅dr⃗\displaystyle\int_{-C}\vec{F}\cdot d\vec{r} = -\int_C \vec{F}\cdot d\vec{r}∫−C​F⋅dr=−∫C​F⋅dr
  • Linearity: ∫C(aF⃗+bG⃗)⋅dr⃗=a∫CF⃗⋅dr⃗+b∫CG⃗⋅dr⃗\displaystyle\int_C (a\vec{F}+b\vec{G})\cdot d\vec{r} = a\int_C\vec{F}\cdot d\vec{r} + b\int_C\vec{G}\cdot d\vec{r}∫C​(aF+bG)⋅dr=a∫C​F⋅dr+b∫C​G⋅dr

Practice

5 problems
  1. 1
    Given force field F⃗(x,y)=⟨−y,x⟩\vec{F}(x,y)=\langle-y,x\rangleF(x,y)=⟨−y,x⟩, find the work to move an object along the ellipse r⃗(t)=⟨2cos⁡t,3sin⁡t⟩\vec{r}(t)=\langle2\cos t,3\sin t\rangler(t)=⟨2cost,3sint⟩ from (2,0)(2,0)(2,0) to (0,3)(0,3)(0,3).
    no calculator, same as the exam
    Answer3π3\pi3πanswer recomputed · sympy
    1. Work is W=∫CF⃗⋅dr⃗=∫abF⃗(r⃗(t))⋅r⃗ ′(t) dt\displaystyle W=\int_C\vec F\cdot d\vec r=\int_a^b\vec F(\vec r(t))\cdot\vec r\,{}'(t)\,dtW=∫C​F⋅dr=∫ab​F(r(t))⋅r′(t)dt.
    2. Find the ttt-range from the endpoints: (2,0)(2,0)(2,0) is t=0t=0t=0 and (0,3)(0,3)(0,3) is t=π2t=\tfrac\pi2t=2π​, so we travel a quarter of the ellipse.
    3. On CCC: F⃗(r⃗(t))=⟨−y,x⟩=⟨−3sin⁡t, 2cos⁡t⟩\vec F(\vec r(t))=\langle-y,x\rangle=\langle-3\sin t,\,2\cos t\rangleF(r(t))=⟨−y,x⟩=⟨−3sint,2cost⟩ and r⃗ ′(t)=⟨−2sin⁡t, 3cos⁡t⟩\vec r\,{}'(t)=\langle-2\sin t,\,3\cos t\rangler′(t)=⟨−2sint,3cost⟩.
    4. Dot them: 6sin⁡2t+6cos⁡2t=66\sin^2t+6\cos^2t=66sin2t+6cos2t=6 — the integrand is constant.
    5. Set up: W=∫0π/26 dt=6⋅π2=3π\displaystyle W=\int_0^{\pi/2}6\,dt=6\cdot\frac{\pi}{2}=3\piW=∫0π/2​6dt=6⋅2π​=3π.

    TrapReaching for Green's theorem. CCC is an open quarter-arc, not a closed curve, so Green does not apply; and F⃗=⟨−y,x⟩\vec F=\langle-y,x\rangleF=⟨−y,x⟩ is not conservative (Py=−1≠1=QxP_y=-1\ne1=Q_xPy​=−1=1=Qx​), so the path genuinely matters and FTLI is off the table. You must integrate along this arc.

  2. 2
    Compute the flux of F⃗(x,y)=⟨x,y⟩\vec{F}(x,y)=\langle x,y\rangleF(x,y)=⟨x,y⟩ across the curve r⃗(t)=⟨3cos⁡t,2sin⁡t⟩\vec{r}(t)=\langle3\cos t,2\sin t\rangler(t)=⟨3cost,2sint⟩, −π≤t≤π-\pi\le t\le\pi−π≤t≤π. (Flux =∫CP dy−Q dx=\displaystyle\int_C P\,dy-Q\,dx=∫C​Pdy−Qdx.)

Fundamental Theorem of Line Integrals

Lesson 28 · §17.3
Don't know this yet? §s173 in the full guide →
From the official study guide

Fundamental Theorem of Line Integrals

If F⃗=∇f\vec{F} = \nabla fF=∇f (conservative) and CCC goes from AAA to BBB:

∫C∇f⋅dr⃗=f(B)−f(A)\int_C \nabla f \cdot d\vec{r} = f(B) - f(A)∫C​∇f⋅dr=f(B)−f(A)

Independence of Path

∫CF⃗⋅dr⃗\displaystyle\int_C \vec{F}\cdot d\vec{r}∫C​F⋅dr is path-independent if and only if F⃗\vec{F}F is conservative.

Closed Curves

∮CF⃗⋅dr⃗=0  ⟺  F⃗ is conservative\oint_C \vec{F}\cdot d\vec{r} = 0 \iff \vec{F} \text{ is conservative}∮C​F⋅dr=0⟺F is conservative

Finding the Potential Function

Given F⃗=⟨P,Q⟩\vec{F} = \langle P, Q \rangleF=⟨P,Q⟩ is conservative:

  • Integrate PPP with respect to xxx to get f(x,y)=∫P dx+g(y)f(x,y) = \int P\,dx + g(y)f(x,y)=∫Pdx+g(y)
  • Differentiate with respect to yyy and set equal to QQQ to find g′(y)g'(y)g′(y), then integrate

Green's Theorem

Lesson 29 · §17.4
Don't know this yet? §s174 in the full guide →
From the official study guide

Green's Theorem

Let CCC be a positively oriented (counterclockwise), simple closed curve bounding region DDD:

∮CP dx+Q dy=∬D(∂Q∂x−∂P∂y)dA\oint_C P\,dx + Q\,dy = \iint_D \left(\frac{\partial Q}{\partial x} - \frac{\partial P}{\partial y}\right)dA∮C​Pdx+Qdy=∬D​(∂x∂Q​−∂y∂P​)dA

Area via Green's Theorem

A=∮Cx dy=−∮Cy dx=12∮Cx dy−y dxA = \oint_C x\,dy = -\oint_C y\,dx = \frac{1}{2}\oint_C x\,dy - y\,dxA=∮C​xdy=−∮C​ydx=21​∮C​xdy−ydx

Note: Green's theorem converts a difficult line integral into a double integral, or vice versa.

Practice

5 problems

    2. Read off P=xP=xP=x and Q=x2+y2Q=x^2+y^2Q=x2+y2. The orientation is already CCW, so no sign flip is needed.
    3. ∂Q∂x=2x\dfrac{\partial Q}{\partial x}=2x∂x∂Q​=2x and ∂P∂y=0\dfrac{\partial P}{\partial y}=0∂y∂P​=0, so the integrand is just 2x2x2x.
    4. RRR is the rectangle 0≤x≤20\le x\le20≤x≤2, 0≤y≤30\le y\le30≤y≤3 — a genuine rectangle, so the limits are constants and the order does not matter.
    5. ∬R2x dA=∫03 ⁣ ⁣∫022x dx dy=∫03[x2]02dy=∫034 dy=12\displaystyle\iint_R 2x\,dA=\int_0^3\!\!\int_0^2 2x\,dx\,dy=\int_0^3\left[x^2\right]_0^2 dy=\int_0^3 4\,dy=12∬R​2xdA=∫03​∫02​2xdxdy=∫03​[x2]02​dy=∫03​4dy=12.

    TrapTrying to parametrize all four sides by hand. That is four integrals, and the ∫x dx\int x\,dx∫xdx pieces on the top and bottom edges cancel in a way that is easy to botch — one sign slip on the *return* edges (which run right-to-left and top-to-bottom) and you get 000 or 242424. Green's theorem exists precisely to make the orientation bookkeeping automatic; use it. Also note P=xP=xP=x contributes nothing, since Py=0P_y=0Py​=0 — the whole answer comes from QQQ.

14

Curl and Divergence

Lesson 30 · §17.5
Don't know this yet? §s175 in the full guide →
From the official study guide

Curl

For F⃗=⟨P,Q,R⟩\vec{F} = \langle P, Q, R \rangleF=⟨P,Q,R⟩:

curl F⃗=∇×F⃗=∣i⃗j⃗k⃗∂x∂y∂zPQR∣=⟨Ry−Qz, Pz−Rx, Qx−Py⟩\text{curl}\,\vec{F} = \nabla \times \vec{F} = \begin{vmatrix}\vec{i} & \vec{j} & \vec{k} \\ \partial_x & \partial_y & \partial_z \\ P & Q & R\end{vmatrix} = \left\langle R_y - Q_z,\, P_z - R_x,\, Q_x - P_y \right\ranglecurlF=∇×F=​i∂x​P​j​∂y​Q​k∂z​R​​=⟨Ry​−Qz​,Pz​−Rx​,Qx​−Py​⟩

Divergence

div F⃗=∇⋅F⃗=∂P∂x+∂Q∂y+∂R∂z\text{div}\,\vec{F} = \nabla \cdot \vec{F} = \frac{\partial P}{\partial x} + \frac{\partial Q}{\partial y} + \frac{\partial R}{\partial z}divF=∇⋅F=∂x∂P​+∂y∂Q​+∂z∂R​

Key Identities

  • F⃗\vec{F}F conservative ⇒\Rightarrow⇒ curl F⃗=0⃗\text{curl}\,\vec{F} = \vec{0}curlF=0
  • div(curl F⃗)=0\text{div}(\text{curl}\,\vec{F}) = 0div(curlF)=0 always
  • curl(∇f)=0⃗\text{curl}(\nabla f) = \vec{0}curl(∇f)=0 always (gradient fields are irrotational)

    AnswerConservative; φ=xyz+C\varphi=xyz+Cφ=xyz+Cprose answer · not machine-checkable
    1. Test with the curl. P=yzP=yzP=yz, Q=xzQ=xzQ=xz, R=xyR=xyR=xy.
    2. Ry−Qz=x−x=0R_y-Q_z=x-x=0Ry​−Qz​=x−x=0;   Pz−Rx=y−y=0\;P_z-R_x=y-y=0Pz​−Rx​=y−y=0;   Qx−Py=z−z=0\;Q_x-P_y=z-z=0Qx​−Py​=z−z=0. So curl⁡F⃗=0⃗\operatorname{curl}\vec F=\vec 0curlF=0, and since F⃗\vec FF is a polynomial field on all of R3\mathbb R^3R3 (simply connected), F⃗\vec FF is conservative.
    3. Now build φ\varphiφ with ∇φ=F⃗\nabla\varphi=\vec F∇φ=F. Start from φx=yz\varphi_x=yzφx​=yz and integrate in xxx, treating y,zy,zy,z as constants: φ=xyz+g(y,z)\varphi=xyz+g(y,z)φ=xyz+g(y,z) — the 'constant' of integration may depend on the other variables.
    4. Differentiate that in yyy: φy=xz+gy(y,z)\varphi_y=xz+g_y(y,z)φy​=xz+gy​(y,z). Match against Q=xzQ=xzQ=xz, so gy=0g_y=0gy​=0 and g=h(z)g=h(z)g=h(z).
    5. Differentiate in zzz: φz=xy+h′(z)\varphi_z=xy+h'(z)φz​=xy+h′(z). Match against R=xyR=xyR=xy, so h′(z)=0h'(z)=0h′(z)=0 and hhh is a genuine constant.
    6. φ=xyz+C\varphi=xyz+Cφ=xyz+C, and one checks ∇(xyz)=⟨yz,xz,xy⟩=F⃗\nabla(xyz)=\langle yz,xz,xy\rangle=\vec F∇(xyz)=⟨yz,xz,xy⟩=F.

    TrapWriting the first antiderivative as φ=xyz+C\varphi=xyz+Cφ=xyz+C with a numeric constant. At that stage the unknown is a whole function g(y,z)g(y,z)g(y,z), because anything free of xxx dies under ∂x\partial_x∂x​. Collapsing it to a number too early means you never actually verify φy=Q\varphi_y=Qφy​=Q and φz=R\varphi_z=Rφz​=R — on a field where the components do *not* fit together, that shortcut produces a 'potential' for a non-conservative field. Also: test with curl⁡\operatorname{curl}curl, not div⁡\operatorname{div}div. Here div⁡F⃗=0\operatorname{div}\vec F=0divF=0 too, but that says the field is incompressible, an entirely different statement.

  5. 5
    Find div⁡F⃗\operatorname{div}\vec{F}divF for F⃗=⟨exy,eyz,exz⟩\vec{F}=\langle e^{xy},e^{yz},e^{xz}\rangleF=⟨exy,eyz,exz⟩, and verify the identity div⁡(curl⁡G⃗)=0\operatorname{div}(\operatorname{curl}\vec{G})=0div(curlG)=0 for any smooth G⃗\vec{G}G.
    no calculator, same as the exam
    Answerdiv⁡F⃗=yexy+zeyz+xexz\operatorname{div}\vec{F}=ye^{xy}+ze^{yz}+xe^{xz}divF=yexy+zeyz+xexzanswer recomputed · sympy
    1. div⁡F⃗=∇⋅F⃗=Px+Qy+Rz\operatorname{div}\vec F=\nabla\cdot\vec F=P_x+Q_y+R_zdivF=∇⋅F=Px​+Qy​+Rz​ — each component differentiated with respect to its own variable, summed to a scalar.
    2. P=exyP=e^{xy}P=exy, so Px=yexyP_x=ye^{xy}Px​=yexy (chain rule: ∂x(xy)=y\partial_x(xy)=y∂x​(xy)=y).
    3. Q=eyzQ=e^{yz}Q=eyz, so Qy=zeyzQ_y=ze^{yz}Qy​=zeyz.
    4. R=exzR=e^{xz}R=exz, so Rz=xexzR_z=xe^{xz}Rz​=xexz.
    5. div⁡F⃗=yexy+zeyz+xexz\operatorname{div}\vec F=ye^{xy}+ze^{yz}+xe^{xz}divF=yexy+zeyz+xexz.
    6. For the identity, let G⃗=⟨G1,G2,G3⟩\vec G=\langle G_1,G_2,G_3\rangleG=⟨G1​,G2​,G3​⟩. Then curl⁡G⃗=⟨∂yG3−∂zG2,  ∂zG1−∂xG3,  ∂xG2−∂yG1⟩\operatorname{curl}\vec G=\langle \partial_yG_3-\partial_zG_2,\;\partial_zG_1-\partial_xG_3,\;\partial_xG_2-\partial_yG_1\ranglecurlG=⟨∂y​G3​−∂z​G2​,∂z​G1​−∂x​G3​,∂x​G2​−∂y​G1​⟩.
    7. div⁡(curl⁡G⃗)=(G3yx−G2zx)+(G1zy−G3xy)+(G2xz−G1yz)\operatorname{div}(\operatorname{curl}\vec G)=\left(G_{3yx}-G_{2zx}\right)+\left(G_{1zy}-G_{3xy}\right)+\left(G_{2xz}-G_{1yz}\right)div(curlG)=(G3yx​−G2zx​)+(G1zy​−G3xy​)+(G2xz​−G1yz​).
    8. By Clairaut's theorem the mixed partials commute (G3yx=G3xyG_{3yx}=G_{3xy}G3yx​=G3xy​, etc.), so the six terms cancel in pairs and div⁡(curl⁡G⃗)=0\operatorname{div}(\operatorname{curl}\vec G)=0div(curlG)=0 for every G⃗\vec GG with continuous second partials.

    TrapDropping the chain-rule factor. ∂xexy=yexy\partial_x e^{xy}=ye^{xy}∂x​exy=yexy, not exye^{xy}exy — the answer exy+eyz+exze^{xy}+e^{yz}+e^{xz}exy+eyz+exz is the single most common version of this and it is wrong in all three terms. Watch which variable owns which exponent: the third component is exze^{xz}exz and gets ∂z\partial_z∂z​, producing xexzx e^{xz}xexz, not zexzz e^{xz}zexz. For the identity, the cancellation needs continuous second partials (Clairaut); it is a theorem, not algebra, and the practical payoff is that a field with div⁡H⃗≠0\operatorname{div}\vec H\ne0divH=0 can never be written as curl⁡\operatorname{curl}curl of anything.

Surface Integrals

Lessons 31–33 · §17.6
Don't know this yet? §s176p · §s176a · §s176f in the full guide →
From the official study guide

Surface Integral of a Scalar Function

For surface z=g(x,y)z = g(x,y)z=g(x,y) over region DDD:

∬Sf(x,y,z) dS=∬Df(x,y,g(x,y))gx2+gy2+1 dA\iint_S f(x,y,z)\,dS = \iint_D f(x,y,g(x,y))\sqrt{g_x^2 + g_y^2 + 1}\,dA∬S​f(x,y,z)dS=∬D​f(x,y,g(x,y))gx2​+gy2​+1​dA

Surface Area

A(S)=∬SdS=∬Dgx2+gy2+1 dAA(S) = \iint_S dS = \iint_D \sqrt{g_x^2 + g_y^2 + 1}\,dAA(S)=∬S​dS=∬D​gx2​+gy2​+1​dA

Flux Integral (Surface Integral of a Vector Field)

For F⃗=⟨P,Q,R⟩\vec{F} = \langle P, Q, R \rangleF=⟨P,Q,R⟩ and oriented surface SSS with unit normal n^\hat{n}n^:

∬SF⃗⋅dS⃗=∬SF⃗⋅n^ dS\iint_S \vec{F}\cdot d\vec{S} = \iint_S \vec{F}\cdot\hat{n}\,dS∬S​F⋅dS=∬S​F⋅n^dS

For z=g(x,y)z = g(x,y)z=g(x,y) with upward orientation (n^\hat{n}n^ pointing upward):

∬SF⃗⋅dS⃗=∬D(−Pgx−Qgy+R)dA\iint_S \vec{F}\cdot d\vec{S} = \iint_D \left(-P g_x - Q g_y + R\right)dA∬S​F⋅dS=∬D​(−Pgx​−Qgy​+R)dA

Parametric Surface

For surface r⃗(u,v)\vec{r}(u,v)r(u,v):

∬Sf dS=∬Df(r⃗(u,v)) ∣r⃗u×r⃗v∣ dA\iint_S f\,dS = \iint_D f(\vec{r}(u,v))\,|\vec{r}_u \times \vec{r}_v|\,dA∬S​fdS=∬D​f(r(u,v))∣ru​×rv​∣dA
∬SF⃗⋅dS⃗=∬DF⃗(r⃗(u,v))⋅(r⃗u×r⃗v) dA\iint_S \vec{F}\cdot d\vec{S} = \iint_D \vec{F}(\vec{r}(u,v))\cdot(\vec{r}_u \times \vec{r}_v)\,dA∬S​F⋅dS=∬D​F(r(u,v))⋅(ru​×rv​)dA

    Answer5305\sqrt{30}530​answer recomputed · sympy
    1. Solve for zzz to get the surface as a graph: z=g(x,y)=10−2x−5yz=g(x,y)=10-2x-5yz=g(x,y)=10−2x−5y.
    2. For a graph, dS=1+gx2+gy2  dAdS=\sqrt{1+g_x^2+g_y^2}\;dAdS=1+gx2​+gy2​​dA. Here gx=−2g_x=-2gx​=−2, gy=−5g_y=-5gy​=−5, so dS=1+4+25 dA=30 dAdS=\sqrt{1+4+25}\,dA=\sqrt{30}\,dAdS=1+4+25​dA=30​dA — a constant, as it must be for a plane.
    3. Find the shadow DDD. The first octant needs x≥0x\ge0x≥0, y≥0y\ge0y≥0, and z≥0z\ge0z≥0, and the last of these is 10−2x−5y≥010-2x-5y\ge010−2x−5y≥0, i.e. 2x+5y≤102x+5y\le102x+5y≤10.
    4. DDD is the triangle with legs along the axes: xxx-intercept x=5x=5x=5, yyy-intercept y=2y=2y=2. Its area is 12(5)(2)=5\tfrac12(5)(2)=521​(5)(2)=5.
    5. Area=∬D30 dA=30⋅area(D)=530\displaystyle\text{Area}=\iint_D\sqrt{30}\,dA=\sqrt{30}\cdot\text{area}(D)=5\sqrt{30}Area=∬D​30​dA=30​⋅area(D)=530​.
    6. Explicitly: ∫05 ⁣ ⁣∫0(10−2x)/530 dy dx=530\displaystyle\int_0^5\!\!\int_0^{(10-2x)/5}\sqrt{30}\,dy\,dx=5\sqrt{30}∫05​∫0(10−2x)/5​30​dydx=530​.

    TrapReporting 555 — the area of the shadow — by forgetting the 1+gx2+gy2\sqrt{1+g_x^2+g_y^2}1+gx2​+gy2​​ factor. A tilted plane is always larger than its projection, so the stretch factor is ≥1\ge1≥1 and your answer must exceed the shadow's area. The other trap is the shadow's shape: the first octant condition z≥0z\ge0z≥0 is what bounds DDD, giving the triangle 2x+5y≤102x+5y\le102x+5y≤10 with intercepts x=5x=5x=5, y=2y=2y=2. Students who integrate over 0≤x≤50\le x\le50≤x≤5, 0≤y≤20\le y\le20≤y≤2 (the full rectangle) double the answer to 103010\sqrt{30}1030​.

For this field that gives ∫(−9cos⁡tsin⁡t+4sin⁡tcos⁡t)dt=0\int(-9\cos t\sin t+4\sin t\cos t)dt=0∫(−9costsint+4sintcost)dt=0, a plausible-looking but wrong answer. SSS is a flat horizontal disk at height z=1z=1z=1, oriented upward, so the unit normal is simply n^=k⃗=⟨0,0,1⟩\hat n=\vec k=\langle0,0,1\ranglen^=k=⟨0,0,1⟩ and dS⃗=⟨0,0,1⟩ dAd\vec S=\langle0,0,1\rangle\,dAdS=⟨0,0,1⟩dA (the graph z=g=1z=g=1z=g=1 has gx=gy=0g_x=g_y=0gx​=gy​=0, so dS=dAdS=dAdS=dA).
    2. Dot the field with the normal: F⃗⋅n^=⟨y,−x,1⟩⋅⟨0,0,1⟩=1\vec F\cdot\hat n=\langle y,-x,1\rangle\cdot\langle0,0,1\rangle=1F⋅n^=⟨y,−x,1⟩⋅⟨0,0,1⟩=1. Only the k⃗\vec kk-component of F⃗\vec FF survives.
    3. ∬SF⃗⋅dS⃗=∬x2+y2≤11 dA=area of the unit disk=π\displaystyle\iint_S\vec F\cdot d\vec S=\iint_{x^2+y^2\le1}1\,dA=\text{area of the unit disk}=\pi∬S​F⋅dS=∬x2+y2≤1​1dA=area of the unit disk=π.
    4. Explicitly in polar: ∫02π ⁣ ⁣∫011⋅r dr dθ=2π⋅12=π\displaystyle\int_0^{2\pi}\!\!\int_0^1 1\cdot r\,dr\,d\theta=2\pi\cdot\tfrac12=\pi∫02π​∫01​1⋅rdrdθ=2π⋅21​=π.

    TrapTrying to integrate the yyy and −x-x−x components. They are entirely tangential to a horizontal disk and contribute nothing to flux — this field swirls *within* the plane z=1z=1z=1 and never crosses it. (Its curl is ⟨0,0,−2⟩\langle0,0,-2\rangle⟨0,0,−2⟩, so its *circulation* around the boundary is −2π-2\pi−2π, a completely different number that this problem is baiting you toward.) The second trap is orientation: 'oriented upward' fixes n^=+k⃗\hat n=+\vec kn^=+k; downward would give −π-\pi−π. Third, the disk has radius 111, so its area is π\piπ, not 2π2\pi2π.
